title: AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report
gist: ECB survey data show euro area AI use at work doubled from 26% (2024) to 52% (2026), with median users saving 3 hours/week, but only about half of workers use and benefit from AI, and reported time-savings translate into a much smaller economy-wide efficiency gain (~3.8%) once non-adopters and non-savers are counted.

insights.claim: Euro area workplace AI use doubled in two years, rising from 26% of workers in 2024 to 41% in 2025 and 52% in 2026, per the ECB's Consumer Expectations Survey of roughly 20,000 people across 11 euro area countries.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A majority-adoption threshold has now been crossed in the euro area labor market, which should start showing up in aggregate productivity statistics; watch subsequent CES waves for whether the growth rate holds or plateaus.
insights.quote: the share of workers using AI on the job has doubled from 26% of survey respondents in 2024 to 41% in 2025, reaching 52% in 2026
insights.locator: AI adoption continues to increase in the workplace

insights.claim: Among euro area workers who use AI at work, average usage is about three days per week.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Usage intensity, not just adoption headcount, matters for estimating aggregate time-savings and productivity impact.
insights.locator: A majority of workers now report using AI for work

insights.claim: There is a large education-based adoption gap in AI use at work: 61% of highly educated euro area workers use AI versus 37% of those with lower education levels, and younger workers are about 20 percentage points more likely to use AI than older colleagues.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Uneven adoption by education and age implies uneven productivity and wage-growth effects across the workforce, a potential driver of widening inequality that policymakers should target with training.
insights.quote: adoption among highly educated people reached 61%, compared with 37% among those with lower levels of education
insights.locator: Unsurprisingly, AI adoption varies across demographic groups

insights.claim: Once workers start using AI, usage intensity converges across demographic groups (2.5 to 2.9 days per week on average), meaning the real adoption gap is about whether people start using AI at all, not how heavily they use it once they do.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Policy and employer interventions should focus on getting non-users to try AI at all, since usage habits are similar once the initial adoption barrier is crossed.
insights.quote: with group averages between 2.5 and 2.9 days
insights.locator: Interestingly, once workers open the door to AI

insights.claim: The median euro area worker who uses AI at work reports saving three hours per week, equivalent to about 7.7% of median working time, though the distribution is highly skewed with most users seeing moderate gains and a small minority seeing very large gains.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A skewed distribution means average productivity claims for AI can be misleading; investors modeling AI's macro productivity effect should use median/distributional data, not simple averages.
insights.quote: the median user reports saving three hours per week, or about 7.7% of median working time
insights.locator: AI boosts productivity at work

insights.claim: Because only 48.8% of euro area workers report both using AI and saving time with it, the effective economy-wide efficiency gain from AI is closer to 3.8% of working hours rather than the 7.7% seen among active AI users.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Macro productivity forecasts based on AI must discount user-level time-savings by the adoption rate; roughly half the reported micro-level gain should be applied at the whole-economy level.
insights.quote: for the whole economy, the overall efficiency gain (in other words, the share of savings in working hours attributed to the use of AI) is closer to 3.8%
insights.locator: only half of workers reported using and saving time thanks to AI

insights.claim: The ECB's reported time-savings from AI are notably higher than an earlier Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis study by Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin and David J. Deming, likely because that study capped reported time-savings at four hours while the ECB's Consumer Expectations Survey allowed responses up to 15 hours.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
insights.so_what: Cross-study comparisons of AI productivity estimates require checking survey question design (response caps, geography) before treating headline numbers as comparable.
insights.quote: The St. Louis Fed study limited reported time-savings to a maximum of four hours, whereas respondents to the Consumer Expectations Survey could either specify the exact number of hours saved or select a bracket of up to 15 hours.
insights.locator: However, reported time-savings in our data are higher

insights.claim: Reported time-savings from AI translate into actual productivity gains only if workers redirect freed-up hours into additional output rather than less productive activities, and only if employers are able to put that extra capacity to use.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: This is the key conversion assumption between worker-reported time-savings and GDP-level productivity growth; if firms cannot absorb freed capacity, headline AI adoption stats will overstate realized productivity.
insights.locator: these time-savings only translate into higher productivity

insights.claim: Literature estimates of additional annual productivity growth from AI over a ten-year horizon range from 0.1% to 3.4%, per an OECD review (Filippucci et al., 2025, G7 economies), while separate ECB research puts the euro area figure at around 0.35 percentage points per year on average.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The ECB's own euro area estimate (0.35pp/year) sits toward the low-to-middle end of the broad academic range, useful as a benchmark for euro area potential-growth and inflation forecasting models.
insights.quote: current estimates for additional annual productivity growth from AI over a ten-year period range between 0.1% and 3.4%
insights.locator: In comparison, current estimates for additional annual productivity growth

insights.claim: Generating or debugging code delivers the largest AI time-savings for euro area workers, nearly eight hours per week, yet only around 8% of workers use AI for this purpose, meaning the biggest productivity wins come from a narrow, specialized use case rather than the most common applications.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Firms and investors should look at coding/technical-task AI penetration rather than headline adoption rates as the leading indicator of realized productivity upside; expanding coding-tool usage further has outsized ROI relative to broadening general use.
insights.quote: Generating or debugging code yields the largest gains, at nearly eight hours per week, although only around 8% of workers use AI for this purpose
insights.locator: Efficiency gains delivered by AI vary considerably by task

insights.claim: Data analysis, automation of routine tasks, and creating audio or visual content show the same pattern as coding: high per-user time-savings but comparatively low adoption rates among euro area workers.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: These are the next-highest-leverage AI use cases for productivity after coding; employer training programs targeting these tasks should yield above-average returns.
insights.locator: A similar pattern emerges for data analysis, automation of routine tasks

insights.claim: Research, information gathering, writing and text editing are the most frequently cited AI use cases among euro area workers, but they deliver considerably lower time-savings than more technical tasks like coding.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Most current AI usage is concentrated in lower-value-add tasks; a shift in usage mix toward technical/automation tasks would be a bullish signal for future measured productivity growth even without further adoption growth.
insights.quote: research, information gathering, writing and text editing are among the most frequently cited uses. Yet time-savings reported for these tasks are considerably lower
insights.locator: By contrast, research, information gathering, writing and text editing

insights.claim: Managers show the highest AI adoption rate, the largest time-savings, and the most positive sentiment about AI among euro area occupations, forming a self-reinforcing loop of usage and enthusiasm that positions them to drive further workplace AI rollout.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Employer AI-rollout strategies should leverage manager buy-in and visibility as a change-management lever, since managers are both the heaviest users and the most persuadable champions.
insights.quote: managers use AI the most, save the most time in doing so and ultimately have the most positive perception of the technology; this places them in a good position to help steer AI adoption
insights.locator: For most professions, workers do not see perceived efficiency gains

insights.claim: Occupations with the highest AI adoption rates also tend to save the most hours and hold the most positive views of the technology, suggesting adoption, realized benefit and sentiment reinforce each other rather than adoption alone driving skepticism or fear.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: This virtuous-cycle pattern implies that once an occupation crosses an adoption threshold, further uptake and productivity gains within that group may compound, favoring already-AI-heavy sectors for continued efficiency gains.
insights.locator: The occupations that have the highest adoption rates

themes.theme: Sentiment Decline and Its Economic Undertone

insights.claim: Despite adoption rising, the share of euro area workers viewing AI positively fell from 43% a year ago to 41% now, indicating adoption growth and sentiment are decoupling rather than moving together.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Rising AI usage does not guarantee rising public/worker approval; a souring sentiment trend alongside continued adoption could presage political or regulatory friction even as productivity gains accrue.
insights.quote: the percentage of workers who viewed it positively dropped from 43% to 41%
insights.locator: Overall, AI is perceived less favourably today than one year ago

insights.claim: Workers' views on AI correlate with their broader economic expectations: those with negative AI opinions also report higher expected unemployment one year ahead, greater fear of job loss, and weaker income and spending expectations, suggesting AI sentiment surveys partly capture general economic pessimism rather than AI-specific views alone.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: AI-sentiment indicators should be read alongside broader consumer-confidence data; a drop in AI sentiment may be signaling macro pessimism more than a specific AI backlash, which matters for interpreting future survey waves.
insights.quote: Workers who hold negative opinions on AI are also more pessimistic about the economy, reporting higher expectations of unemployment one year ahead, greater fear of job loss and weaker expectations for income growth and spending
insights.locator: This might be connected to an uncertain economic environment more broadly

insights.claim: So far there is no evidence that AI has reduced total employment at the firm level in the euro area, even as adoption has grown rapidly.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: This directly counters the strongest bearish labor-market narrative around AI job displacement, at least in current euro area firm-level data; a shift in this finding in future ECB releases would be a significant macro signal to watch.
insights.quote: there is no evidence of AI reducing total employment at the firm level
insights.locator: However, so far, there is no evidence of AI reducing total employment

insights.claim: Workers' fear of being replaced by AI rises when general labor market prospects are weaker, implying that job-loss anxiety attributed to AI is partly a function of the broader labor market cycle rather than AI adoption itself.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A weakening euro area labor market could amplify AI-replacement fears independent of any actual change in AI capability or deployment, a distinction relevant for policymakers designing communication and retraining responses.
insights.quote: the fear of being replaced by AI increases when labour market prospects are generally less favourable
insights.locator: And the fear of being replaced by AI increases

insights.claim: Roughly half of euro area workers still do not use AI at work despite two years of rapid adoption growth, leaving a large untapped pool for future productivity gains if barriers are addressed.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The remaining non-adopter half represents the primary upside case for further AI-driven productivity growth in the euro area over coming years.
insights.quote: roughly half of workers still do not use AI
insights.locator: Barriers to AI adoption remain

insights.claim: About one-third of non-adopting euro area workers say AI is irrelevant to their current tasks, while 41% overall (34% of managers) report simply having no interest in using AI, alongside concerns about accuracy/reliability and lack of employer provision.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A large share of non-adoption is attitudinal (disinterest) rather than purely structural (task irrelevance or tool access), meaning training and demonstrated-usefulness campaigns may be more impactful than simply expanding tool access.
insights.quote: 41% are uninterested in using AI (34% of managers)
insights.locator: One-third of respondents do not use AI because it is irrelevant

insights.claim: About half of euro area workers say better training and a better understanding of AI's usefulness would encourage them to start using it, identifying training as the single most cited lever for boosting adoption.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Training investment is the highest-leverage single intervention for closing the adoption gap, more so than tool distribution or mandates.
insights.quote: around half of all workers point to better training on using AI tools and a better understanding of AI’s usefulness
insights.locator: When asked what would encourage them to adopt AI

themes.theme: Employer Response and Policy Path Forward

insights.claim: About half of euro area firms plan to invest in AI training over the next 12 months according to the latest SAFE survey wave, directly addressing workers' most-cited barrier to adoption, but the other half are not investing, partly linked to a third of managers being insufficiently interested in AI themselves.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Firm-level training investment intentions (SAFE survey) are a leading indicator to track for future AI-driven productivity acceleration; a rising share of firms investing in training would signal closing of the adoption gap.
insights.quote: About half of firms plan to invest in AI training over the next 12 months
insights.locator: Employers appear to be responding to some of these needs

insights.claim: The ECB concludes that recent recovery in euro area aggregate productivity growth may already partly reflect AI-driven time-savings, even though gains remain uneven across tasks and occupations, and that employers and national authorities should prioritize worker training and easier tool access to unlock further productivity potential.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: This is an explicit ECB signal linking AI adoption to the euro area productivity growth outlook, relevant for potential-growth and monetary-policy-relevant productivity assumptions, and flags training/tool-access policy as the key lever to watch.
insights.quote: These savings might, even if only partially, be already partly visible in aggregate productivity growth numbers, which have been recovering in the euro area in recent quarters.
insights.locator: Conclusion: boosting productivity to full potential

top_entities: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
